Review of Vectors

Lesson 1 · §13.1-13.4
Don't know this yet? §13.1 · §13.2 · §13.3 · §13.3 · §13.4 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Vector Notation and Operations

A vector has both magnitude (length) and direction. Vector notation:

v⃗=⟨v1,v2,v3⟩orv⃗=v1i⃗+v2j⃗+v3k⃗\vec{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \rangle \quad \text{or} \quad \vec{v} = v_1\vec{i} + v_2\vec{j} + v_3\vec{k}v=⟨v1​,v2​,v3​⟩orv=v1​i+v2​j​+v3​k

where i⃗=⟨1,0,0⟩\vec{i} = \langle 1,0,0 \ranglei=⟨1,0,0⟩, j⃗=⟨0,1,0⟩\vec{j} = \langle 0,1,0 \ranglej​=⟨0,1,0⟩, k⃗=⟨0,0,1⟩\vec{k} = \langle 0,0,1 \ranglek=⟨0,0,1⟩ are the standard basis vectors.

Basic Operations

  • Addition: u⃗+v⃗=⟨u1+v1,u2+v2,u3+v3⟩\vec{u} + \vec{v} = \langle u_1+v_1, u_2+v_2, u_3+v_3 \rangleu+v=⟨u1​+v1​,u2​+v2​,u3​+v3​⟩
  • Scalar multiplication: cu⃗=⟨cu1,cu2,cu3⟩c\vec{u} = \langle cu_1, cu_2, cu_3 \ranglecu=⟨cu1​,cu2​,cu3​⟩
  • Vector from P to Q: PQ→=⟨x2−x1,y2−y1,z2−z1⟩\overrightarrow{PQ} = \langle x_2-x_1, y_2-y_1, z_2-z_1 \ranglePQ​=⟨x2​−x1​,y2​−y1​,z2​−z1​⟩

Magnitude and Unit Vectors

Magnitude (Length) of vector v⃗=⟨v1,v2,v3⟩\vec{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \ranglev=⟨v1​,v2​,v3​⟩:

∣v⃗∣=v12+v22+v32|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}∣v∣=v12​+v22​+v32​​

A unit vector is a vector of length 1. The unit vector in the direction of v⃗\vec{v}v is:

v^=v⃗∣v⃗∣\hat{v} = \frac{\vec{v}}{|\vec{v}|}v^=∣v∣v​

Dot Product

Dot Product of u⃗=⟨u1,u2,u3⟩\vec{u} = \langle u_1, u_2, u_3 \rangleu=⟨u1​,u2​,u3​⟩ and v⃗=⟨v1,v2,v3⟩\vec{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \ranglev=⟨v1​,v2​,v3​⟩:

u⃗⋅v⃗=u1v1+u2v2+u3v3=∣u⃗∣∣v⃗∣cos⁡θ\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3 = |\vec{u}||\vec{v}|\cos\thetau⋅v=u1​v1​+u2​v2​+u3​v3​=∣u∣∣v∣cosθ

where θ\thetaθ is the angle between the vectors. Result is a scalar.

  • u⃗⋅v⃗=0⟺\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = 0 \Longleftrightarrowu⋅v=0⟺ vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal)
  • Angle between vectors: cos⁡θ=u⃗⋅v⃗∣u⃗∣∣v⃗∣\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v}}{|\vec{u}||\vec{v}|}cosθ=∣u∣∣v∣u⋅v​

Cross Product

Cross Product of u⃗=⟨u1,u2,u3⟩\vec{u} = \langle u_1, u_2, u_3 \rangleu=⟨u1​,u2​,u3​⟩ and v⃗=⟨v1,v2,v3⟩\vec{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \ranglev=⟨v1​,v2​,v3​⟩:

u⃗×v⃗=∣i⃗j⃗k⃗u1u2u3v1v2v3∣=⟨u2v3−u3v2,u3v1−u1v3,u1v2−u2v1⟩\vec{u} \times \vec{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \vec{i} & \vec{j} & \vec{k} \\ u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{vmatrix} = \langle u_2v_3-u_3v_2, u_3v_1-u_1v_3, u_1v_2-u_2v_1 \rangleu×v=​iu1​v1​​j​u2​v2​​ku3​v3​​​=⟨u2​v3​−u3​v2​,u3​v1​−u1​v3​,u1​v2​−u2​v1​⟩

Result is a vector perpendicular to both u⃗\vec{u}u and v⃗\vec{v}v.

  • ∣u⃗×v⃗∣=∣u⃗∣∣v⃗∣sin⁡θ|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}| = |\vec{u}||\vec{v}|\sin\theta∣u×v∣=∣u∣∣v∣sinθ = area of parallelogram formed by u⃗\vec{u}u and v⃗\vec{v}v
  • u⃗×v⃗=0⃗⟺\vec{u} \times \vec{v} = \vec{0} \Longleftrightarrowu×v=0⟺ vectors are parallel
  • u⃗×v⃗=−(v⃗×u⃗)\vec{u} \times \vec{v} = -(\vec{v} \times \vec{u})u×v=−(v×u) (anti-commutative)

Lines and Planes in Space

Lesson 2 · §13.5
Don't know this yet? §13.5 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Equations of a Line

Line through point P0(x0,y0,z0)P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)P0​(x0​,y0​,z0​) with direction vector v⃗=⟨a,b,c⟩\vec{v} = \langle a, b, c \ranglev=⟨a,b,c⟩:

Vector Equation

r⃗(t)=r⃗0+tv⃗=⟨x0,y0,z0⟩+t⟨a,b,c⟩\vec{r}(t) = \vec{r}_0 + t\vec{v} = \langle x_0, y_0, z_0 \rangle + t\langle a, b, c \rangler(t)=r0​+tv=⟨x0​,y0​,z0​⟩+t⟨a,b,c⟩

Parametric Equations

x=x0+at,y=y0+bt,z=z0+ctx = x_0 + at, \quad y = y_0 + bt, \quad z = z_0 + ctx=x0​+at,y=y0​+bt,z=z0​+ct

Symmetric Equations (if a,b,c≠0a, b, c \neq 0a,b,c=0)

x−x0a=y−y0b=z−z0c\frac{x-x_0}{a} = \frac{y-y_0}{b} = \frac{z-z_0}{c}ax−x0​​=by−y0​​=cz−z0​​

Equation of a Plane

Plane through point P0(x0,y0,z0)P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)P0​(x0​,y0​,z0​) with normal vector n⃗=⟨a,b,c⟩\vec{n} = \langle a, b, c \ranglen=⟨a,b,c⟩:

a(x−x0)+b(y−y0)+c(z−z0)=0a(x-x_0) + b(y-y_0) + c(z-z_0) = 0a(x−x0​)+b(y−y0​)+c(z−z0​)=0

or equivalently: ax+by+cz=dax + by + cz = dax+by+cz=d, where d=ax0+by0+cz0d = ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0d=ax0​+by0​+cz0​

Finding Normal Vectors

  • If two direction vectors v⃗1\vec{v}_1v1​ and v⃗2\vec{v}_2v2​ lie in the plane, then n⃗=v⃗1×v⃗2\vec{n} = \vec{v}_1 \times \vec{v}_2n=v1​×v2​
  • If given three points, use two vectors formed by the points

Note: Angle between two planes equals the angle between their normal vectors.

Practice

6 problems
  1. 1
    The line through (1,3,−1)(1, 3, -1)(1,3,−1) and (3,1,2)(3, 1, 2)(3,1,2) intersects the plane x+y+z=6x + y + z = 6x+y+z=6 at what point?
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer(3, 1, 2)(3,\, 1,\, 2)(3,1,2)answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Direction: v⃗=⟨3−1, 1−3, 2−(−1)⟩=⟨2,−2,3⟩\vec v=\langle3-1,\,1-3,\,2-(-1)\rangle=\langle2,-2,3\ranglev=⟨3−1,1−3,2−(−1)⟩=⟨2,−2,3⟩.
    2. Line: r⃗(t)=⟨1+2t,  3−2t,  −1+3t⟩\vec r(t)=\langle 1+2t,\;3-2t,\;-1+3t\rangler(t)=⟨1+2t,3−2t,−1+3t⟩.
    3. Substitute into x+y+z=6x+y+z=6x+y+z=6: (1+2t)+(3−2t)+(−1+3t)=3+3t=6⇒t=1(1+2t)+(3-2t)+(-1+3t)=3+3t=6\Rightarrow t=1(1+2t)+(3−2t)+(−1+3t)=3+3t=6⇒t=1.
    4. r⃗(1)=⟨3,1,2⟩\vec r(1)=\langle3,1,2\rangler(1)=⟨3,1,2⟩ — the second given point happens to lie on the plane.

    TrapSign errors in the direction vector. Notice the xxx and yyy parameters cancel, so the whole equation collapses to 3+3t3+3t3+3t; if yours does not collapse, recheck v⃗\vec vv.

  2. 2
    Find the equation of the plane containing (2,1,−1)(2, 1, -1)(2,1,−1) and parallel to the vectors ⟨1,0,3⟩\langle 1, 0, 3 \rangle⟨1,0,3⟩ and ⟨2,1,0⟩\langle 2, 1, 0 \rangle⟨2,1,0⟩.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer−3x+6y+z+1=0-3x + 6y + z + 1 = 0−3x+6y+z+1=0answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Two vectors parallel to the plane give the normal through a cross product.
    2. n⃗=⟨1,0,3⟩×⟨2,1,0⟩=⟨0⋅0−3⋅1,  3⋅2−1⋅0,  1⋅1−0⋅2⟩=⟨−3,6,1⟩\vec n=\langle1,0,3\rangle\times\langle2,1,0\rangle=\langle 0\cdot0-3\cdot1,\;3\cdot2-1\cdot0,\;1\cdot1-0\cdot2\rangle=\langle-3,6,1\ranglen=⟨1,0,3⟩×⟨2,1,0⟩=⟨0⋅0−3⋅1,3⋅2−1⋅0,1⋅1−0⋅2⟩=⟨−3,6,1⟩.
    3. Point-normal form at (2,1,−1)(2,1,-1)(2,1,−1): −3(x−2)+6(y−1)+1(z+1)=0-3(x-2)+6(y-1)+1(z+1)=0−3(x−2)+6(y−1)+1(z+1)=0.
    4. Expand: −3x+6+6y−6+z+1=0⇒−3x+6y+z+1=0-3x+6+6y-6+z+1=0\Rightarrow -3x+6y+z+1=0−3x+6+6y−6+z+1=0⇒−3x+6y+z+1=0.

    Trap'Parallel to the vectors' does not mean the vectors are normals. They lie *in* the plane; their cross product is the normal.

03

Quadric Surfaces

Lessons 3-4 · §13.6
Don't know this yet? §13.6 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

A quadric surface is the graph of a second-degree equation in three variables.

Standard Quadric Surfaces
Surface Standard Equation Key Features
Ellipsoid x2a2+y2b2+z2c2=1\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1a2x2​+b2y2​+c2z2​=1 All traces are ellipses
Elliptic Paraboloid z=x2a2+y2b2z = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}z=a2x2​+b2y2​ Opens upward (or downward if negative)
Hyperbolic Paraboloid z=x2a2−y2b2z = \frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2}z=a2x2​−b2y2​ Saddle shape
Hyperboloid (1 sheet) x2a2+y2b2−z2c2=1\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1a2x2​+b2y2​−c2z2​=1 Connected, one piece
Hyperboloid (2 sheets) z2c2−x2a2−y2b2=1\frac{z^2}{c^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1c2z2​−a2x2​−b2y2​=1 Two separate pieces
Elliptic Cone z2c2=x2a2+y2b2\frac{z^2}{c^2} = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}c2z2​=a2x2​+b2y2​ Double cone, vertex at origin

Identifying Quadric Surfaces

  • Look at which variables are squared
  • Check the signs (all positive, mixed signs, or one isolated)
  • Check what the equation equals (0, 1, or a variable)
  • Sketch traces in the coordinate planes (xy, xz, yz)

Traces are curves of intersection with planes parallel to coordinate planes.

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1
    Identify the surface: −x2+y24−z29=1\displaystyle -x^2 + \frac{y^2}{4} - \frac{z^2}{9} = 1−x2+4y2​−9z2​=1.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    AnswerHyperboloid of two sheets (axis along yyy)prose answer · not machine-checkable
    1. Write it with the positive term first: y24−x2−z29=1\dfrac{y^2}{4}-x^2-\dfrac{z^2}{9}=14y2​−x2−9z2​=1.
    2. One positive square, two negative, equals +1+1+1 — that is the two-sheet signature.
    3. Trace at y=0y=0y=0: −x2−z29=1-x^2-\frac{z^2}{9}=1−x2−9z2​=1, impossible. Nothing at the origin, so it cannot be one connected sheet.
    4. Hyperboloid of two sheets, axis along yyy — the axis is always the variable whose square is positive.

    TrapOne sheet vs two sheets is decided by the count of minus signs, not by which variable is isolated. One minus = one sheet (connected); two minuses = two sheets.

  2. 2
    Identify the surface defined by x2+4x+y2−2y+z2=−4x^2 + 4x + y^2 - 2y + z^2 = -4x2+4x+y2−2y+z2=−4. (Hint: complete the square.)
    no calculator, same as the exam
    AnswerSphere centered at (−2, 1, 0)(-2,\, 1,\, 0)(−2,1,0) with radius 111answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Complete the square in xxx and yyy: x2+4x=(x+2)2−4x^2+4x=(x+2)^2-4x2+4x=(x+2)2−4 and y2−2y=(y−1)2−1y^2-2y=(y-1)^2-1y2−2y=(y−1)2−1.
    2. (x+2)2−4+(y−1)2−1+z2=−4(x+2)^2-4+(y-1)^2-1+z^2=-4(x+2)2−4+(y−1)2−1+z2=−4.
    3. (x+2)2+(y−1)2+z2=1(x+2)^2+(y-1)^2+z^2=1(x+2)2+(y−1)2+z2=1.
    4. Sphere, centre (−2,1,0)(-2,1,0)(−2,1,0), radius 111.

    TrapMoving the completion constants the wrong way. The −4-4−4 and −1-1−1 come out on the left, so they get added to the right: −4+4+1=1-4+4+1=1−4+4+1=1.

  3. 3
    Identify the surface: z=4x2+9y2z = 4x^2 + 9y^2z=4x2+9y2.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    AnswerElliptic paraboloid opening upwardprose answer · not machine-checkable
    1. One variable (zzz) appears to the first power, the other two are squared with the same sign.
    2. That is the paraboloid family. Both coefficients positive ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ opens upward.
    3. Traces z=k>0z=k>0z=k>0 are ellipses 4x2+9y2=k4x^2+9y^2=k4x2+9y2=k; traces x=0x=0x=0 and y=0y=0y=0 are upward parabolas.
    4. Elliptic paraboloid opening upward.

  4. 4
    Describe the trace of x24+y29−z2=1\displaystyle \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{9} - z^2 = 14x2​+9y2​−z2=1 in the plane z=2z = 2z=2.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    AnswerEllipse: x220+y245=1\dfrac{x^2}{20} + \dfrac{y^2}{45} = 120x2​+45y2​=1answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Set z=2z=2z=2: x24+y29−4=1\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}-4=14x2​+9y2​−4=1.
    2. x24+y29=5\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=54x2​+9y2​=5.
    3. Divide by 555: x220+y245=1\dfrac{x^2}{20}+\dfrac{y^2}{45}=120x2​+45y2​=1 — an ellipse.

  5. 5
    Identify the surface: x2+y24=z29\displaystyle x^2 + \frac{y^2}{4} = \frac{z^2}{9}x2+4y2​=9z2​.

04

Vector-Valued Functions

Lesson 5 · §14.1
Don't know this yet? §14.1 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Definition

A vector-valued function (or vector function) has the form:

r⃗(t)=⟨f(t),g(t),h(t)⟩=f(t)i⃗+g(t)j⃗+h(t)k⃗\vec{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t) \rangle = f(t)\vec{i} + g(t)\vec{j} + h(t)\vec{k}r(t)=⟨f(t),g(t),h(t)⟩=f(t)i+g(t)j​+h(t)k

The graph is a space curve traced out as t varies.

Limits and Continuity

The limit of a vector function is computed component-wise:

lim⁡t→ar⃗(t)=⟨lim⁡t→af(t),lim⁡t→ag(t),lim⁡t→ah(t)⟩\lim_{t \to a} \vec{r}(t) = \left\langle \lim_{t \to a} f(t), \lim_{t \to a} g(t), \lim_{t \to a} h(t) \right\ranglet→alim​r(t)=⟨t→alim​f(t),t→alim​g(t),t→alim​h(t)⟩

05

Calculus of Vector-Valued Functions & Motion in Space

Lessons 6-7 · §14.2-14.3
Don't know this yet? §14.2 · §14.3 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Derivative

r⃗′(t)=lim⁡h→0r⃗(t+h)−r⃗(t)h=⟨f′(t),g′(t),h′(t)⟩\vec{r}'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\vec{r}(t+h) - \vec{r}(t)}{h} = \langle f'(t), g'(t), h'(t) \rangler′(t)=h→0lim​hr(t+h)−r(t)​=⟨f′(t),g′(t),h′(t)⟩

Integral

∫r⃗(t) dt=⟨∫f(t) dt,∫g(t) dt,∫h(t) dt⟩+C⃗\int \vec{r}(t)\,dt = \left\langle \int f(t)\,dt, \int g(t)\,dt, \int h(t)\,dt \right\rangle + \vec{C}∫r(t)dt=⟨∫f(t)dt,∫g(t)dt,∫h(t)dt⟩+C

Differentiation Rules

For vector functions u⃗(t)\vec{u}(t)u(t) and v⃗(t)\vec{v}(t)v(t):

  • ddt[u⃗(t)+v⃗(t)]=u⃗′(t)+v⃗′(t)\frac{d}{dt}[\vec{u}(t) + \vec{v}(t)] = \vec{u}'(t) + \vec{v}'(t)dtd​[u(t)+v(t)]=u′(t)+v′(t)
  • ddt[cu⃗(t)]=cu⃗′(t)\frac{d}{dt}[c\vec{u}(t)] = c\vec{u}'(t)dtd​[cu(t)]=cu′(t)
  • ddt[f(t)u⃗(t)]=f′(t)u⃗(t)+f(t)u⃗′(t)\frac{d}{dt}[f(t)\vec{u}(t)] = f'(t)\vec{u}(t) + f(t)\vec{u}'(t)dtd​[f(t)u(t)]=f′(t)u(t)+f(t)u′(t)
  • ddt[u⃗(t)⋅v⃗(t)]=u⃗′(t)⋅v⃗(t)+u⃗(t)⋅v⃗′(t)\frac{d}{dt}[\vec{u}(t) \cdot \vec{v}(t)] = \vec{u}'(t) \cdot \vec{v}(t) + \vec{u}(t) \cdot \vec{v}'(t)dtd​[u(t)⋅v(t)]=u′(t)⋅v(t)+u(t)⋅v′(t)
  • ddt[u⃗(t)×v⃗(t)]=u⃗′(t)×v⃗(t)+u⃗(t)×v⃗′(t)\frac{d}{dt}[\vec{u}(t) \times \vec{v}(t)] = \vec{u}'(t) \times \vec{v}(t) + \vec{u}(t) \times \vec{v}'(t)dtd​[u(t)×v(t)]=u′(t)×v(t)+u(t)×v′(t)

Motion in Space

If r⃗(t)\vec{r}(t)r(t) is the position vector at time t:

  • Velocity: v⃗(t)=r⃗′(t)\vec{v}(t) = \vec{r}'(t)v(t)=r′(t)
  • Speed: ∣v⃗(t)∣=∣r⃗′(t)∣|\vec{v}(t)| = |\vec{r}'(t)|∣v(t)∣=∣r′(t)∣
  • Acceleration: a⃗(t)=v⃗′(t)=r⃗′′(t)\vec{a}(t) = \vec{v}'(t) = \vec{r}''(t)a(t)=v′(t)=r′′(t)

Unit Tangent Vector

T⃗(t)=r⃗′(t)∣r⃗′(t)∣=v⃗(t)∣v⃗(t)∣\vec{T}(t) = \frac{\vec{r}'(t)}{|\vec{r}'(t)|} = \frac{\vec{v}(t)}{|\vec{v}(t)|}T(t)=∣r′(t)∣r′(t)​=∣v(t)∣v(t)​

Practice

    2. ∫⟨2t,3,−1⟩dt=⟨t2, 3t, −t⟩+C⃗\int\langle2t,3,-1\rangle dt=\langle t^2,\,3t,\,-t\rangle+\vec C∫⟨2t,3,−1⟩dt=⟨t2,3t,−t⟩+C.

06

Arc Length and Curvature

Lesson 8 · §14.4-14.5
Don't know this yet? §14.4 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Arc Length

Arc Length of curve r⃗(t)\vec{r}(t)r(t) from t=at = at=a to t=bt = bt=b:

L=∫ab∣r⃗′(t)∣ dt=∫ab[f′(t)]2+[g′(t)]2+[h′(t)]2 dtL = \int_a^b |\vec{r}'(t)|\,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{[f'(t)]^2 + [g'(t)]^2 + [h'(t)]^2}\,dtL=∫ab​∣r′(t)∣dt=∫ab​[f′(t)]2+[g′(t)]2+[h′(t)]2​dt

Arc Length Function

s(t)=∫t0t∣r⃗′(u)∣ dus(t) = \int_{t_0}^t |\vec{r}'(u)|\,dus(t)=∫t0​t​∣r′(u)∣du

Curvature

Curvature measures how quickly the curve changes direction:

κ=∣dT⃗ds∣=∣T⃗′(t)∣∣r⃗′(t)∣=∣r⃗′(t)×r⃗′′(t)∣∣r⃗′(t)∣3\kappa = \left|\frac{d\vec{T}}{ds}\right| = \frac{|\vec{T}'(t)|}{|\vec{r}'(t)|} = \frac{|\vec{r}'(t) \times \vec{r}''(t)|}{|\vec{r}'(t)|^3}κ=​dsdT​​=∣r′(t)∣∣T′(t)∣​=∣r′(t)∣3∣r′(t)×r′′(t)∣​

For a plane curve y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x):

κ(x)=∣f′′(x)∣[1+(f′(x))2]3/2\kappa(x) = \frac{|f''(x)|}{[1+(f'(x))^2]^{3/2}}κ(x)=[1+(f′(x))2]3/2∣f′′(x)∣​

07

Functions of Several Variables

Lesson 9 · §15.1
Don't know this yet? §15.1 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Definition

A function of two variables assigns to each ordered pair (x, y) in a set D a unique real number z=f(x,y)z = f(x,y)z=f(x,y).

Visualization Methods

  • Graph: Surface in 3D space
  • Level Curves: Curves in xy-plane where f(x,y)=kf(x,y) = kf(x,y)=k (constant)
  • Contour Map: Collection of level curves

Functions of Three Variables

For w=f(x,y,z)w = f(x,y,z)w=f(x,y,z):

  • Level Surfaces: Surfaces where f(x,y,z)=kf(x,y,z) = kf(x,y,z)=k

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1
    Find the domain of f(x,y)=9−x2−y2f(x, y) = \sqrt{9 - x^2 - y^2}f(x,y)=9−x2−y2​.

    Answer{(x,y): x2+y2≤9}\{(x,y):\, x^2+y^2 \le 9\}{(x,y):x2+y2≤9}prose answer · not machine-checkable
    1. A square root needs a non-negative radicand: 9−x2−y2≥09-x^2-y^2\ge09−x2−y2≥0.
    2. x2+y2≤9x^2+y^2\le9x2+y2≤9.
    3. The closed disk of radius 333 centred at the origin, boundary included.

    TrapWriting a strict inequality. The boundary circle is fine — it just makes f=0f=0f=0 there. Strictness belongs to logs and denominators.

    1. Set x2+4y2=kx^2+4y^2=kx2+4y2=k. For k<0k<0k<0 there are no points; k=0k=0k=0 is the single point at the origin.
    2. For k>0k>0k>0, divide: x2k+y2k/4=1\dfrac{x^2}{k}+\dfrac{y^2}{k/4}=1kx2​+k/4y2​=1.
    3. Ellipses centred at the origin, twice as wide as they are tall (semi-axes k\sqrt kk​ and k/2\sqrt k/2k​/2).

08

Limits and Continuity

Lesson 10 · §15.2
Don't know this yet? §15.2 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Limits

We write lim⁡(x,y)→(a,b)f(x,y)=L\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y) \to (a,b)} f(x,y) = L(x,y)→(a,b)lim​f(x,y)=L, if f(x,y) approaches L as (x,y) approaches (a,b) from any direction.

Proving a Limit Does Not Exist

Find two different paths that give different limits:

  • Along x-axis: y=0y = 0y=0
  • Along y-axis: x=0x = 0x=0
  • Along y=xy = xy=x or y=mxy = mxy=mx
  • Along parabolic paths: y=x2y = x^2y=x2

Continuity

f is continuous at (a,b) if:

lim⁡(x,y)→(a,b)f(x,y)=f(a,b)\lim_{(x,y) \to (a,b)} f(x,y) = f(a,b)(x,y)→(a,b)lim​f(x,y)=f(a,b)

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1
    Evaluate lim⁡(x,y)→(0,0)x3yx4+y2\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y) \to (0,0)} \frac{x^3 y}{x^4 + y^2}(x,y)→(0,0)lim​x4+y2x3y​, or show it does not exist.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Official answerlimit does not existchecked · official answer wrong
    Correct answer000recomputed · sympy
    1. Try paths first. Along y=0y=0y=0: 000. Along x=0x=0x=0: 000. Along y=x2y=x^2y=x2: x3⋅x2x4+x4=x2→0\frac{x^3\cdot x^2}{x^4+x^4}=\frac{x}{2}\to0x4+x4x3⋅x2​=2x​→0. Every path gives 000, which is a signal to stop hunting and start proving.
    2. Squeeze. By AM–GM, x4+y2≥2x2∣y∣x^4+y^2\ge 2x^2|y|x4+y2≥2x2∣y∣, so for (x,y)≠(0,0)(x,y)\ne(0,0)(x,y)=(0,0):
    3. ∣x3yx4+y2∣≤∣x∣3∣y∣2x2∣y∣=∣x∣2.\left|\frac{x^3y}{x^4+y^2}\right|\le\frac{|x|^3|y|}{2x^2|y|}=\frac{|x|}{2}.​x4+y2x3y​​≤2x2∣y∣∣x∣3∣y∣​=2∣x∣​.
    4. ∣x∣2→0\frac{|x|}{2}\to02∣x∣​→0, so the limit exists and equals 000.

    TrapA finite pile of paths never proves a limit exists — but it also never proves it fails. When every path you try agrees, switch to a bound.

    The official answer is wrongThe official answer says the limit does not exist. It does: the AM–GM squeeze above bounds the expression by ∣x∣2\frac{|x|}{2}2∣x∣​. (Compare x2yx4+y2\frac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}x4+y2x2y​, which genuinely fails along y=x2y=x^2y=x2 — one power of xxx away.)

    Evaluate lim⁡(x,y)→(0,0)3x2yx2+y2\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y) \to (0,0)} \frac{3x^2 y}{x^2 + y^2}(x,y)→(0,0)lim​x2+y23x2y​, or show it does not exist.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Official answerlimit does not existchecked · official answer wrong
    Correct answer000recomputed · sympy
    1. Every path gives 000: along y=mxy=mxy=mx, 3x2(mx)x2(1+m2)=3mx1+m2→0\frac{3x^2(mx)}{x^2(1+m^2)}=\frac{3mx}{1+m^2}\to0x2(1+m2)3x2(mx)​=1+m23mx​→0.
    2. Squeeze, and this one is immediate: x2≤x2+y2x^2\le x^2+y^2x2≤x2+y2, so x2x2+y2≤1\dfrac{x^2}{x^2+y^2}\le1x2+y2x2​≤1 and
    3. ∣3x2yx2+y2∣≤3∣y∣.\left|\frac{3x^2y}{x^2+y^2}\right|\le 3|y|.​x2+y23x2y​​≤3∣y∣.
    4. 3∣y∣→03|y|\to03∣y∣→0 as (x,y)→(0,0)(x,y)\to(0,0)(x,y)→(0,0), so the limit exists and equals 000.

    TrapDegree counting is the fast check: the numerator is degree 333, the denominator degree 222. Numerator degree strictly larger ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ the quotient is squeezed to 000. Only equal degrees can produce a path-dependent limit.

    The official answer is wrongThe official answer says the limit does not exist. It does: it is 000, by the one-line bound ∣3x2yx2+y2∣≤3∣y∣\left|\frac{3x^2y}{x^2+y^2}\right|\le3|y|​x2+y23x2y​​≤3∣y∣. The classic DNE example is xyx2+y2\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}x2+y2xy​ — numerator and denominator both degree 222.

Partial Derivatives

Lesson 11 · §15.3
Don't know this yet? §15.3 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

First-Order Partial Derivatives

Partial derivative with respect to x (treat y as constant):

∂f∂x=fx=lim⁡h→0f(x+h,y)−f(x,y)h\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = f_x = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h,y) - f(x,y)}{h}∂x∂f​=fx​=h→0lim​hf(x+h,y)−f(x,y)​

Partial derivative with respect to y (treat x as constant):

∂f∂y=fy=lim⁡h→0f(x,y+h)−f(x,y)h\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = f_y = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x,y+h) - f(x,y)}{h}∂y∂f​=fy​=h→0lim​hf(x,y+h)−f(x,y)​

Higher-Order Partial Derivatives

  • fxx=∂2f∂x2f_{xx} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}fxx​=∂x2∂2f​
  • fyy=∂2f∂y2f_{yy} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2}fyy​=∂y2∂2f​
  • fxy=∂2f∂y∂xf_{xy} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x}fxy​=∂y∂x∂2f​
  • fyx=∂2f∂x∂yf_{yx} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y}fyx​=∂x∂y∂2f​

Clairaut's Theorem

If fxyf_{xy}fxy​ and fyxf_{yx}fyx​ are both continuous:

fxy=fyxf_{xy} = f_{yx}fxy​=fyx​

The Chain Rule

Lesson 12 · §15.4
Don't know this yet? §15.4 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Chain Rule - Case 1

If z=f(x,y)z = f(x,y)z=f(x,y) where x=g(t)x = g(t)x=g(t) and y=h(t)y = h(t)y=h(t):

dzdt=∂f∂xdxdt+∂f∂ydydt\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}dtdz​=∂x∂f​dtdx​+∂y∂f​dtdy​

Chain Rule - Case 2

If z=f(x,y)z = f(x,y)z=f(x,y) where x=g(s,t)x = g(s,t)x=g(s,t) and y=h(s,t)y = h(s,t)y=h(s,t):

∂z∂s=∂f∂x∂x∂s+∂f∂y∂y∂s\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}∂s∂z​=∂x∂f​∂s∂x​+∂y∂f​∂s∂y​

Implicit Differentiation

If F(x,y,z)=0F(x,y,z) = 0F(x,y,z)=0 defines z implicitly:

∂z∂x=−FxFz,∂z∂y=−FyFz\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}, \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_z}∂x∂z​=−Fz​Fx​​,∂y∂z​=−Fz​Fy​​

Directional Derivatives & Gradient

Lesson 13 · §15.5
Don't know this yet? §15.5 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Directional Derivative

The directional derivative Du⃗f(a,b)D_{\vec{u}}f(a,b)Du​f(a,b) measures rate of change in direction of unit vector u⃗\vec{u}u:

Du⃗f(a,b)=∇f(a,b)⋅u⃗=fx(a,b)u1+fy(a,b)u2D_{\vec{u}}f(a,b) = \nabla f(a,b) \cdot \vec{u} = f_x(a,b)u_1 + f_y(a,b)u_2Du​f(a,b)=∇f(a,b)⋅u=fx​(a,b)u1​+fy​(a,b)u2​

Gradient Vector

∇f(x,y)=⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩\nabla f(x,y) = \langle f_x(x,y), f_y(x,y) \rangle∇f(x,y)=⟨fx​(x,y),fy​(x,y)⟩

Properties of the Gradient

  • ∇f\nabla f∇f points in direction of maximum rate of increase
  • ∣∇f∣|\nabla f|∣∇f∣ gives the maximum rate of increase
  • −∇f-\nabla f−∇f points in direction of maximum decrease
  • ∇f\nabla f∇f is orthogonal to level curves

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1

Tangent Planes & Linear Approximation

Lesson 14 · §15.6
Don't know this yet? §15.6 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Tangent Plane

Equation of tangent plane to z=f(x,y)z = f(x,y)z=f(x,y) at (a,b,f(a,b))(a, b, f(a,b))(a,b,f(a,b)):

z=f(a,b)+fx(a,b)(x−a)+fy(a,b)(y−b)z = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)z=f(a,b)+fx​(a,b)(x−a)+fy​(a,b)(y−b)

Linear Approximation

L(x,y)=f(a,b)+fx(a,b)(x−a)+fy(a,b)(y−b)L(x,y) = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)L(x,y)=f(a,b)+fx​(a,b)(x−a)+fy​(a,b)(y−b)

Differential

dz=fx dx+fy dydz = f_x\,dx + f_y\,dydz=fx​dx+fy​dy

Normal Vector

For z=f(x,y)z = f(x,y)z=f(x,y): n⃗=⟨fx,fy,−1⟩\vec{n} = \langle f_x, f_y, -1 \ranglen=⟨fx​,fy​,−1⟩

For F(x,y,z)=0F(x,y,z) = 0F(x,y,z)=0: n⃗=∇F=⟨Fx,Fy,Fz⟩\vec{n} = \nabla F = \langle F_x, F_y, F_z \ranglen=∇F=⟨Fx​,Fy​,Fz​⟩

Maximum and Minimum Problems

Lessons 15-16 · §15.7
Don't know this yet? §15.7 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Critical Points

Point (a,b) is a critical point if:

fx(a,b)=0 and fy(a,b)=0(∇f(a,b)=0⃗)f_x(a,b) = 0 \text{ and } f_y(a,b) = 0 \quad (\nabla f(a,b) = \vec{0})fx​(a,b)=0 and fy​(a,b)=0(∇f(a,b)=0)

Second Derivative Test

Let the discriminant be:

D=fxx(a,b)fyy(a,b)−[fxy(a,b)]2D = f_{xx}(a,b)f_{yy}(a,b) - [f_{xy}(a,b)]^2D=fxx​(a,b)fyy​(a,b)−[fxy​(a,b)]2

Classification

  • If D>0D > 0D>0 and fxx>0f_{xx} > 0fxx​>0: local minimum
  • If D>0D > 0D>0 and fxx<0f_{xx} < 0fxx​<0: local maximum
  • If D<0D < 0D<0: saddle point
  • If D=0D = 0D=0: inconclusive

Absolute Max/Min on Closed Region

Step 1: Find all critical points inside region D

Step 2: Find extreme values on the boundary of D

Step 3: Compare all values - largest is absolute max, smallest is absolute min

Practice

    4. The geometry backs it up: along y=0y=0y=0 the surface is x2x^2x2 (a valley), along x=0x=0x=0 it is −y2-y^2−y2 (a ridge). This is the standard saddle.

    TrapD<0D<0D<0 is the one case that is fully decisive with no second test needed. Do not go looking at fxxf_{xx}fxx​ afterwards; its sign is irrelevant when D<0D<0D<0.

  6. 6
    Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x,y)=4xy−x2−2y2+2f(x,y) = 4xy - x^2 - 2y^2 + 2f(x,y)=4xy−x2−2y2+2 on the region 0≤x≤20 \le x \le 20≤x≤2, 0≤y≤10 \le y \le 10≤y≤1.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    AnswerAbs. max =4= 4=4 at (2,1)(2,1)(2,1); abs. min =−2= -2=−2 at (2,0)(2,0)(2,0)answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Interior: fx=4y−2x=0f_x=4y-2x=0fx​=4y−2x=0 and fy=4x−4y=0f_y=4x-4y=0fy​=4x−4y=0 give x=yx=yx=y and x=2yx=2yx=2y, so only (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) — a corner, not interior. No interior critical point.
    2. Edge y=0y=0y=0: f=2−x2f=2-x^2f=2−x2 on x∈[0,2]x\in[0,2]x∈[0,2], running from 222 down to −2-2−2.
    3. Edge y=1y=1y=1: f=4x−x2f=4x-x^2f=4x−x2 on [0,2][0,2][0,2], running from 000 up to 444 at x=2x=2x=2.
    4. Edge x=0x=0x=0: f=2−2y2∈[0,2]f=2-2y^2\in[0,2]f=2−2y2∈[0,2]. Edge x=2x=2x=2: f=−2y2+8y−2f=-2y^2+8y-2f=−2y2+8y−2, from −2-2−2 at y=0y=0y=0 to 444 at y=1y=1y=1.
